summary:
Anyone visiting Zamfara stands under two overlapping layers of criminal law. At national level Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct through the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), which the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sex between men under secular law. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that the Act reaches well beyond marriage: it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The statute binds any person present in the country, visitors included.

The second layer is Sharia criminal law, and Zamfara is where it began. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that Zamfara's governor was the first to act, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those twelve remain the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. The Home Office note adds that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Zamfara's own adoption machinery is documented in detail. In June 1999 the state's governor appointed a committee mandated to study implementing Sharia, including the full scope of Islamic criminal law. Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, set out the state's account at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000, describing the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled codification of a Sharia Penal Code. The Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000. The codification of offences and punishments produced the penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against people perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Zamfara's pioneering role gives its arrangements outsized weight: the state introduced Sharia criminal jurisdiction first, and the penal-code architecture its officials codified was then replicated by eleven other northern states, so the framework a visitor encounters in Zamfara is the template for a twelve-state bloc rather than a local variation.

The comparison across the country is unflattering to any assumption of uniformity. A visitor moving from Zamfara to Lagos or Abuja leaves Sharia criminal jurisdiction behind but remains inside the SSMPA's secular reach, with the same exposure of up to 14 years' imprisonment and the same documented police appetite for extortion, as the March 2025 beating of Okafor in Lagos illustrates.

Nigeria's criminalisation is itself layered on colonial-era law, and the SSMPA of 2014 reinforced rather than replaced it; the country's legal order offers LGBTQ+ people no protective statute to counterweight the penal ones.
